what_this_is: The query set for RDR-217 Phase 1's recall measurement. A committed artifact rather than an inline list, because P1.4 re-runs the IDENTICAL set against the hybrid route and a comparison across two different sets would be void. No recall number has been taken with it yet; that is P1.2's job, after P1's review.

corpus_scope.why: Note chunk geometry changed on write at 1be4146da (nexus-b2tld): store_put splits a note at 1,689 characters when the model imposes no window, which is every Voyage collection, and the 257 existing notes over 2,000 characters are NOT re-embedded (Sam's decision). A measurement drawing on knowledge__ notes would therefore straddle a write-side change, with pre-change notes each exactly one chunk and post-change notes one or more. Scoping to code__ sidesteps the window constraint entirely rather than managing it, because that change does not touch file-indexed corpora. The second reason is not defensive: identifier-shaped and rare-token queries are what the lexical leg is FOR, and that population lives in code, so the scope the constraint pushes us to is also the scope the hypothesis wants.
corpus_scope.consequence_to_state_in_the_report: Phase 1's number is therefore about code retrieval. It does NOT license a claim about knowledge notes or prose docs, and Phase 3's surface decision should not be read as validated for those corpora.
corpus_scope.completeness_contract: THE CORPUS PASSED TO THE HARNESS MUST BE COMPLETE FOR THE COLLECTIONS MEASURED, and two known traps in this codebase silently shrink it: paging reads cap at 300 rows per call (limits.MAX_QUERY_RESULTS), and store_get_many truncates each document at 4000 characters by default. A truncated body drops literal tokens and shrinks the ground-truth denominator; a truncated page drops chunks entirely. P1.2's corpus builder must page to exhaustion and read untruncated content, and the report's corpus_fingerprint plus corpus_size are what let a later reader check that two measurements saw the same corpus rather than trust that they did.

ordering.choice: engine order, no client-side re-ranking of any kind
ordering.why: The harness calls HttpVectorClient.search and HttpVectorClient.hybrid_search directly and consumes the row order the engine returns. It does NOT route through search_engine.search_cross_corpus, does not apply the topic boost, the frecency boost, bibliographic weighting or the per-collection distance threshold. This measures the RETRIEVAL leg, which is the thing the hypothesis is about: whether the relevant chunk comes back at all within k. Ranking quality is a different question and is not what unblocks Phase 3.
ordering.why_this_is_stated_rather_than_left_to_a: A sibling instrument got this wrong on 2026-09-19: tests/benchmarks/test_retrieval_drift_gate.py sorted by r.distance after 7b1b49075 moved the topic-boost credit out of that field into r.topic_boost, so the benchmark was blind to the ranking layer by construction and passed at 0.9013 against a 0.9078 baseline while measuring the wrong quantity (fixed in 9c74b3a0b). Not sorting at all is how this harness avoids inheriting that trap: there is no sort key here to fall out of step with a field that moved. If a later phase wants ranking rather than retrieval, it must choose a key deliberately and say so here — max(0.0, distance - topic_boost) is the effective-distance ordering, apply_ranking_boosts is the full reranker.

relevance_model.the_bias_this_carries_and_why_it_is_not_: For an identifier-shaped query, relevance is DEFINED as 'the chunk contains that identifier'. That favours a lexical gate by construction, because a lexical gate is a literal-containment matcher. It is not circular for the query shape it covers — when a developer types resolve_active_session_id, the rows they want ARE the rows containing it, so literal containment is the task definition rather than a thumb on the scale. It WOULD be circular as a claim about retrieval generally. The prose queries exist to keep that honest: they use source-path relevance, which no lexical gate is privileged on, and a Phase 1 report that shows a lexical gain on identifiers and none on prose is the expected and interesting result rather than a disappointment.
relevance_model.what_would_make_this_instrument_wrong: If the prose queries turned out to also be satisfiable by the engine's lexical gate, the contrast would collapse and every shape would favour the lexical leg. The gate is plainto_tsquery OR trigram word_similarity >= 0.6 over the WHOLE query string, so an exact-substring guard is not sufficient to rule this out — a query differing from its needle only by a separator clears the trigram threshold. test_prose_queries_are_not_satisfiable_by_literal_containment therefore normalises separators before comparing, which is what caught prose-01's leak; a stem-level collision remains a judgement call the 'why' field has to carry.
relevance_model.rare_means_rare_in_chunks_not_in_files: A rare-token slot must hold a token appearing in at most k CHUNKS of the measured corpus, and the first version of this set got that wrong in a way only a real run exposed. Rarity was picked from repo-wide grep counts, which count occurrences across files; the harness scores chunks, and k is the window. Measured over the real corpus (src/nexus + tests, production chunker): quarantine_collection_name 17 chunks, mint_test_tenant 19, against k=10. Both were labelled rare and neither was, so the rare-token shape was not being measured at all. mislabelled_rare_tokens() refused the run; the driver's precheck now applies the same test before embedding rather than after.

queries.why: A snake_case function name a developer would type verbatim. Widely referenced (25 files at authoring time), so a miss is not explained by sparsity.
Same shape, different subsystem, so a result is not an artifact of one module's vocabulary.
Carries a digit inside the token (t1), which `english` stemming and subword vector tokenisation treat differently from a pure-alpha name.
Leading underscore, and rare (3 files). The private-name prefix is a token vector embeddings routinely drop and a literal matcher keeps.
CamelCase exception name rather than snake_case, so the set does not measure one casing convention only.
A test-infrastructure name. Its surrounding prose is about staleness and skipping, so a vector search has plausible near-misses to be drawn to.

queries.text: how does a client work out where to send its requests
queries.why: Contrast case, REWRITTEN after the Phase 1 review found a trigram leak. It previously read 'how does the client discover which service endpoint to talk to' against a needle of 'service_endpoint' — one character apart once the separator is normalised. The engine's gate is plainto_tsquery OR trigram word_similarity >= 0.6 (PgVectorRepository.java:1348), so the lexical leg could very plausibly have surfaced this row by leakage rather than by value, collapsing the contrast the whole instrument leans on. The rewrite shares no stem with the needle.

queries.text: what slows things down when an upstream starts refusing requests
queries.why: Contrast case, RETARGETED after the driver's precheck found its ground truth resolving to nothing. It previously pointed at 'build-lease', which is a shell script: the corpus is Python, so no chunk could ever match and the query measured the corpus rather than the route. Now aimed at rate_brake.py, a real Python target whose filename shares no stem with the query text.

queries.text: how much can be written in a single request before it is refused
queries.why: Contrast case, and the one entry this set got WRONG on the first pass. Its text originally read 'where are the limits on how much can be written in one request', which contains its own ground-truth needle verbatim, so the answer was derivable from the query string and a literal matcher would have been privileged on a query whose whole job is to contrast with the identifier shape. test_prose_queries_are_not_satisfiable_by_literal_containment caught it on the first run. The rewritten text names the concept without using the word.

metric.also_reported: recall@k, with its ceiling min(1.0, k/|relevant|) beside it
metric.why_not_recall_as_primary: RECALL@K IS CEILING-CAPPED BY GROUND-TRUTH SIZE, and this corpus makes that fatal rather than academic. Measured on this repo at authoring time: resolve_active_session_id has 122 literal occurrences, publish_t1_session_lease 91, and the token originally used for rare-03 had 681. Against a ground truth of even 50 distinct chunks, recall@10 cannot exceed 0.2 — a route returning ten perfect hits would score 0.2, and the difference between two routes would compress into noise, so a flat result could not be read as 'no headroom'. Precision@k is bounded at 1.0 whatever the ground truth's size and answers the question Phase 1 actually asks: when a developer types an identifier, how much of the returned window is worth reading.
metric.this_is_a_recorded_deviation: The RDR's Phase 1 text says recall. The Phase 1 review (bead nexus-lqo4p.2) raised the ceiling effect as a ship-blocker BEFORE any number was taken, which is exactly what that review is sequenced to do. Changing the primary figure is therefore a review-driven correction, stated here and in T2 rather than swapped in silently.
